questions.q: What is the fundamental difference between a tag and a branch?
options: A tag is a fixed pointer to one commit that never moves; a branch is a pointer that moves forward automatically with new commits
They are identical in every way
A branch can only exist on GitHub, never locally
A tag automatically deletes the commit it points to
questions.explain: Unlike a branch, which advances as new commits land, a tag permanently marks one specific commit — exactly what you want for a release version.

questions.q: What does an annotated tag store that a lightweight tag doesn't?
options: Nothing — they're exactly the same
A message, the tagger's name, a date, and optionally a GPG signature
The entire file contents of the repository
A list of every branch in the repo
questions.explain: An annotated tag is a full Git object storing metadata (message, tagger, date) and can be signed, unlike a lightweight tag which is just a name on a commit.

questions.q: What happens to tags during a plain `git push` with no extra flags?
options: They are automatically pushed along with commits
They are deleted from the local repository
Tags are NOT pushed automatically — you must explicitly push a specific tag or use --tags
They are converted into branches
questions.explain: A regular git push does not send tags to the remote; they require an explicit git push origin <tag> or git push origin --tags.

questions.q: What is a GitHub Release, relative to a tag?
options: A completely unrelated feature with no connection to tags
A wrapper around a tag that adds release notes, source archives, and optional build artifacts
A replacement for tags that makes them obsolete
A tag that can only be created through the command line, never the web UI
questions.explain: A Release wraps an existing (or newly created) tag with documentation and downloadable assets, without changing what the tag itself points to.

questions.q: If you edit a published GitHub release's notes to fix a typo, what happens to the underlying tag and commit?
options: They are both deleted and recreated
The tag automatically moves to a new commit
Nothing — editing a release's notes only changes the documentation, not the tag or the commit it points to
The repository's entire history is rewritten
questions.explain: Release notes are documentation layered on top of a tag; editing them doesn't touch the tag itself or the commit it permanently points to.
